title: Procurement brief — guarantees, isolation, predictable throughput (Dedicated)
body:
Purpose and audience:
This brief is designed for commercial reps, solutions engineers, and procurement teams working with enterprise customers evaluating Redwood Dedicated capacity. It converts technical guarantees into procurement-ready language, highlights negotiation levers, and summarizes competitive positioning around SLAs, tenant isolation, and predictable throughput.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Offer: Redwood Dedicated provides single-tenant GPU pools with contract-backed SLAs for uptime and latency/throughput behavior, plus optional VPC/private control plane for regulatory needs.
- Core guarantees we push in procurement: availability SLA (default 99.95% monthly for dedicated pools), capacity reservation (baseline throughput with burst policy), isolation controls (single-tenant pools, data plane separation, KMS/HSM integration), and transparent fault/fallback playbooks.
- Typical procurement asks we pre-answer: credit calculation, maintenance windows, uplift pricing for strict isolation or geographic residency, and automated fallback to compatible model variants.

Target buyer personas and buying triggers:
- Platform/Cloud Infrastructure (SRE): wants predictable p95/p99 latency and dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
- ML Platform/Product Lead: focused on consistent throughput for model inference SLAs and rollback/fallback policies.
- Procurement/Legal: wants clear SLA definitions, credit mechanics, termination and data retention clauses, and evidence of compliance (SOC2/HIPAA as applicable).

Core positioning pillars (how to talk about it):
1) Predictable economics and performance: "Reserved throughput, predictable unit cost". Emphasize committed baseline, measured tokens/sec and p99 latency targets by model class.
2) Enterprise-grade isolation: "Single-tenant execution with optional VPC and customer-managed keys". Frame as reduced blast radius and compliance-ready deployment model.
3) Operational guarantees, not vague promises: explicit maintenance windows, rollback policies, and documented fallback model families.
4) Procurement-ready terms: short, clear SLA formulas, credit calculations, and a single-attachment template customers can add to their MSA.

SLA and performance language (recommended defaults to include in quotes):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly availability for Dedicated pool control plane and execution endpoints.
- Latency SLO: For small-sequence, chat-style workloads on recommended model family, p95 < 120ms and p99 < 400ms (subject to model & input shape). These are engineering SLOs mapped to contract language (see note on applicability).
- Throughput guarantee: Baseline reserved throughput expressed as X concurrent streams or Y tokens/sec sustained for an agreed model/configuration. Burst capacity available up to Z for short durations (policy and chargeable).
- Credit calculation (example): If Availability < SLA, credit = (SLA - ActualAvailability) / SLA * MonthlyFee, max 50% per month. Credits apply only when customer adheres to recommended request shapes and does not exceed provisioned concurrency without prior notification.
- Maintenance windows: Quarterly maintenance windows (1 × 4-hour window/month or 1 × 6-hour window/quarter) with 72-hour advance notice. Emergency maintenance language limited and defined to critical security incidents only.

Why be specific about latency/throughput in the contract:
- Customers often conflate availability with performance — we separate them. Availability covers service reachability; performance SLOs are scoped to specific model + config + input shapes (we include a runbook demonstrating how to reproduce). This reduces disputes and sets realistic expectations.

Isolation and security (how we describe it to procurement/security):
- Multi-layer isolation options:
  - Logical isolation (default): isolated namespaces, customer-dedicated model caches, and tenant-level network ACLs.
  - Physical isolation (optional paid tier): single-tenant GPU pools with no shared hypervisor or scheduler, physically reserved GPU nodes.
- Networking: VPC peering or private endpoints; optional private control plane to ensure no data plane traversal across public internet.
- Key management: KMS integration and optional HSM for customer-managed keys.
- Compliance artifacts: SOC2 Type II report, audit log export, domain-specific attestations on request (HIPAA addendum, data residency attachments).

Procurement checklist (to attach to quotes):
- Baseline monthly committed capacity (gpus / reserved tokens/sec / concurrency)
- Agreed model families and quantization profile for performance baselining
- Latency/throughput runbook (how metrics are measured, endpoints used)
- SLA table: availability SLA, performance SLOs (scoped), credit mechanics
- Maintenance windows and notification process
- Data handling & retention commitments (logs, inputs, outputs)
- Termination & handover plan (export formats, timeframe)
- Security/compliance attachments (SOC2, penetration test summary, encryption at rest/in transit)

Negotiation levers and pricing guidance for commercial teams:
- Upgrade path: Physical isolation is the most value-add and should carry a significant uplift (20–40% of base dedicated fee depending on capacity scale).
- Commitment discounts: Offer stepped discounts for 12 / 24 / 36 month reservations; longer commitments also reduce ramp T&Cs like the minimum notice for resizing.
- Burst carve-outs: Keep bursts as a metered, pay-as-you-go add-on; this preserves baseline economics while making short-term spikes economical for customers.
- SLA sweeteners: For strategic deals, limit credit cap increases (e.g., raise from 50% to 100% for first 6 months) or include a one-time onboarding credit.

Common procurement objections + rebuttals (short counters for sales use):
- "How do we know the performance numbers you quote will hold for our app?" -> We scope performance SLOs to agreed model/config and reproduce workload samples in our lab; we include a runbook and allow a pre-signing POC to validate.
- "We need guaranteed throughput for peak times." -> We offer committed baseline + burst policy; for strict peaks we recommend an uplifted dedicated pool sized for peak reservation.
- "What about noisy neighbors?" -> Physical single-tenant options eliminate shared scheduling. Logical isolation includes reserved KV caches and request shaping to reduce neighbor impact.

Competitive landscape notes (how to position vs common alternatives):
- Public LLM APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic): Strength = ease of use and model freshness. Weakness = no tenant-dedicated physical pools and limited procurement flexibility for enterprise SLAs and private deployments. Positioning: Redwood gives the same developer ergonomics with enterprise guarantees and predictable economics.
- Cloud-managed endpoints (e.g., AWS/Google managed inference): Strength = deep cloud integrations. Weakness = fragmentation across regions and higher integration ops for model rollouts, and pricing complexity. Positioning: Redwood abstracts the serving runtime with opinionated optimizations and clear model profiles to reduce ops overhead.
- Self-hosted inference stacks (internal infra or OSS runtimes): Strength = total control. Weakness = high engineering TCO and maintenance burden. Positioning: Sell the time-to-market and operational maturity (prefabricated fallbacks, model catalog, rollout controls) and lower total cost of ownership.
- Other inference vendors: call out differences on SLAs and isolation policy (ask for examples and swap-sheet during deal). Keep competitor-specific legal claims out of procurement docs.

Operational playbooks (included as attachments in quotes):
- Onboarding runbook: baseline load test, model calibration, warm-up KV cache steps, and ramp schedule.
- Incident escalation: SRE contact matrix, runbook links, and rollback triggers (e.g., sustained >X% error or p99 latency >Y for Z minutes).
- Fallback model policy: explicit list of compatible fallback variants with acceptable quality degradation matrix and automated routing behavior.

Sample contract clause (procurement-friendly snippet):
"Service Availability. Provider will use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Dedicated Capacity available 99.95% of the time per calendar month, excluding scheduled maintenance and force majeure. If Provider fails to meet the Availability commitment, Customer will be eligible for service credits calculated as: ((SLA - ActualAvailability) / SLA) * MonthlyFee, up to a maximum credit of 50% of the MonthlyFee for the impacted pool. Performance SLOs (e.g., latency and throughput) will be scoped to the model family and input shapes mutually agreed in Appendix A; exceedance of those scoped SLOs will follow the incident remediation and credit mechanics in Appendix B."

Sales attachments recommended to include in every enterprise quote:
- Performance baseline report for quoted model(s) and config
- Onboarding & runbook checklist (ramp plan)
- Draft SLA attachment (editable)
- Isolation and security appendices (VPC, KMS options)

Open questions & follow-ups (for internal GTM):
- Standardize default numeric values for throughput and latency SLOs by model family (action: APPLIED ML to publish by 2026-03-15).
- Build a one-click appendix generator that fills Appendix A (model/config metrics) from onboarding test runs.
- Legal: agree standard maintenance window language and emergency maintenance definition.

Appendix: example quick-quote scenario (for SEs)
- Customer: ecommerce search personalization team; workload: short chat + reranking, 1M requests/day with p95 latency target <150ms.
- Recommended config: 4x A100-equivalent GPU pool, reserved concurrency 200 streams, burst to 400 streams for up to 6 hours/day.
- Contract ask: 12-month reservation, 10% uplift for physical isolation, SLA 99.95%, performance SLO scoped in Appendix A.
- Pricing guidance: baseline monthly fee X, burst metered at Y/1000 tokens, onboarding credit of 1 month for 12-mo deals.

Author note: this doc is intentionally pragmatic — aimed at reducing back-and-forth during commercial cycles. Use the sample clauses and attachments as the starting point for redlines; escalate novel security or residency asks to SRE/infra and Legal early.

Last updated by: Evelyn Zhang (go-to-market) — internal draft for commercial team review.
